suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: getForLogin's cached path drops the login-eligibility guarantee callers relied on, and only one consumer (the bean) was updated.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new cache-backed getForLogin no longer guarantees its returned stream contains only login-eligible IDPs: on a cache hit it re-fetches each cached internal ID via session.identityProviders().getById(id) (line 246) and returns the (organization-aware wrapped) model without re-applying getLoginPredicate(). The old contract that callers could rely on — every returned IdentityProviderModel satisfies the login filters (enabled, hide-on-login, org/public, ...) — is therefore relaxed. This PR compensates in exactly one consumer (OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean now re-checks idp.isEnabled() at lines 75/80), which is evidence the relaxation is real; any other consumer of getForLogin that still trusts the old contract can now receive ineligible IDPs. Re-apply getLoginPredicate() when materializing the cached results in getForLogin (and remove the need for per-caller defensive filters).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Test cleanup removes alias "alias" instead of the created "idp-alias-N" alias, so created IDPs are never cleaned up.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The IDP is created with alias "idp-alias-" + i (and "idp-alias-20" at line 419), but the cleanup callback resolves the alias "alias" instead of the created alias. The result is that the created IDP is never removed during cleanup; `identityProviders().get("alias")` returns the resource for a non-existent alias, so the bound `::remove` will either be a no-op or throw at cleanup time. Use the same alias that was created (e.g. `"idp-alias-" + i` / `"idp-alias-20"`). The same mistake is repeated at line 425.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: LoginFilter javadoc claims to contain all fields considered for login availability, but the new org/BROKER_PUBLIC condition added to getLoginPredicate is not one of the enum's fields.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The javadoc says this enum "contains all fields that are considered when deciding if a provider should be available for login or not", but the predicate changed in this PR (getLoginPredicate, line 254) now considers an additional rule — an organization-linked provider is only eligible when OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC is true — which is not represented by any LoginFilter constant (ENABLED/LINK_ONLY/HIDE_ON_LOGIN). A caller reading only the enum and its doc will compute a different availability set than getLoginPredicate produces. Either add a constant/documenting sentence for the organization-public rule or reword the javadoc to say the enum covers the per-configuration fields while getLoginPredicate adds the organization rule.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Cached branch of getForLogin returns raw models while the uncached branch returns organization-aware wrappers, so results differ by cache state.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `getForLogin` applies `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel` on the uncached return path (lines 218 and 249) but the cached path builds the result from `session.identityProviders().getById(id)` (line 246) and returns it directly (line 254) without the organization-aware mapping. The same call therefore returns models of a different shape depending on cache state, which is the discrepancy the new `idp.isEnabled()` re-check in OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean is compensating for. Apply the same mapping on the cached path (e.g. `.map(this::createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel)`) so both branches agree.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: getForLogin's cached branch returns raw getById models without the org-aware wrapping that the delegate branch (and the consuming bean) assumes.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The cached branch of getForLogin adds `session.identityProviders().getById(id)` directly to the result set, while both the cache-miss and invalidation branches return `idpDelegate.getForLogin(...).map(this::createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel)`. The consumer changed in this PR, OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean (services/.../OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean.java:75,80), documents that it expects the returned IDPs to be wrapped ("re-check isEnabled as idp might have been wrapped"). As written, a cache hit yields unwrapped, org-unaware models and a cache miss yields wrapped models, so the same call returns different shapes depending on cache state. Apply `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel` (or `session.identityProviders().getById(id)` followed by the same mapping) in the cached branch so producer and consumer agree.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Organization/BROKER_PUBLIC condition added to getLoginPredicate is not reflected in the provider's login query used to populate the same caches.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `getLoginPredicate()` now rejects org-linked IDPs unless `BROKER_PUBLIC` is true, and this predicate drives the login-cache invalidation in InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.java:384 and 405. However the fetch that populates those caches goes through the provider's login search options built from ENABLED/LINK_ONLY/HIDE_ON_LOGIN (LoginFilter.getLoginSearchOptions), which were not given the organization/BROKER_PUBLIC test. The validator (predicate) and the generator (query) therefore disagree about which IDPs are login IDPs: an org-linked, non-public IDP is treated as "not a login IDP" for invalidation purposes but can still be returned/populated by the search path. Mirror the organization/BROKER_PUBLIC condition into the query side (or make the search path filter with getLoginPredicate) so both sides classify org IDPs identically.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: New table-widget branch renders an empty table instead of the actual widget data for flagged orgs.
suggestions.suggestionContent:
WHAT: In the new `use-table-widget-visualization` branch, `TableWidgetVisualization` is rendered with hardcoded `columns={[]}` and `tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}}` instead of the actual `result.data`/`result.meta`/`fields`.
WHY: For any organization with the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag, every table widget renders completely empty (no headers, no rows), producing wrong output and hiding the query results the widget is supposed to show.
HOW: Pass the real data, e.g. build columns from `fields`/`fieldAliases` and pass `tableData={{data: result.data, meta: result.meta}}` (or keep the existing StyledSimpleTableChart path until the new visualization is wired up).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Positional zip of error_ids against deduplicated nodestore results can misattribute error details.
suggestions.suggestionContent:
WHAT: `fetch_error_details` builds an ErrorEvent by pairing `error_ids` with `events.values()` via `zip`, i.e. purely by position, while `error_ids` is the key source for `id=event_id`.
WHY: `nodestore.backend.get_multi` deduplicates its id list (`id_list = list(dict.fromkeys(id_list))`, base.py:184), so when `error_ids` contains any duplicate the result dict has fewer entries than `error_ids`; the positional `zip` then shifts and attributes the wrong title/message/timestamp to the remaining ids, emitting incorrect error log lines.
HOW: Iterate the returned mapping instead of zipping: build a `node_id -> event_id` map (as `bulk_fetch_events` already does) and use `for node_id, data in events.items() if data is not None` to look up the event id, avoiding positional coupling.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Falsy-but-valid integer values (0) bypass the age/timestamp cross-field validation.
suggestions.suggestionContent: validate_timestamp and validate_age test the presence of the other field with a truthiness check (`if self.initial_data.get("age")` / `if self.initial_data.get("timestamp")`). Both fields are IntegerField and `timestamp` has `min_value=0`, so 0 is a valid value; `age` also has no min_value, so 0 is allowed. A payload with `age` and `timestamp=0` (or `timestamp` and `age=0`) is therefore wrongly accepted because 0 is falsy. Use explicit presence checks instead, e.g. `if "age" in self.initial_data and self.initial_data["age"] is not None:` (and likewise for timestamp).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: zip(error_ids, events.values()) pairs IDs with event data positionally, assuming get_multi preserves length/order for missing ids.
suggestions.suggestionContent: fetch_error_details builds `node_ids` in `error_ids` order and then does `zip(error_ids, events.values())`, pairing each error id with a value by position. This is only correct if `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a mapping that contains one entry per requested id in the same order (the trailing `if data is not None` filter implies the code expects None placeholders). If the backend omits ids it could not find, `events.values()` is shorter/re-ordered and the zip mis-associates an error id with another event's data, yielding an ErrorEvent with the wrong id/title/message. Iterate the mapping by key and match on the node id (e.g. build a node_id->error_id map and index `events` by key) instead of relying on positional zip.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The new validation-failure branch logs the entire raw, unauthenticated browser report (and returns its errors) instead of a redacted subset.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The added warning path dumps the complete client-supplied report (`raw_report=report`) into the logs. Browser Reporting API payloads are unauthenticated and browser-controlled: `url` can contain query-string secrets/tokens and `body`/`user_agent` are user data. Log only non-sensitive identifiers (report `type` and failing field names), not the whole object; likewise keep the 422 response details limited to field names/messages.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Feature-flag branch renders an empty table, discarding the computed result data used by the fallback.
suggestions.suggestionContent: When `organization.features.includes('use-table-widget-visualization')` is true, this branch renders `TableWidgetVisualization` with hard-coded empty `columns={[]}` and `tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}}`, ignoring the `result.data`, `result.meta`, `fields`, `fieldAliases`, `eventView`, and `fieldHeaderMap` that were computed directly above and are handed to the fallback `StyledSimpleTableChart`. With the flag on, table widgets render as empty tables instead of showing the query results. Pass the computed `result.data`/`result.meta` and derived columns into `TableWidgetVisualization` (or gate the new branch off until it is wired up).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Error id is zipped positionally with get_multi() values, which may not align.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids` and fetches `events = nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)`, then constructs ErrorEvents via `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. This pairs each `event_id` with `data` positionally, assuming `events.values()` is in exactly the same order (and has the same length) as `node_ids`/`error_ids`. If the nodestore backend's `get_multi` does not preserve request order or omits missing keys, the `id` field is attached to the wrong event's title/message/timestamp. Iterate over `node_ids`/`error_ids` and index `events` by node id instead of relying on `values()` ordering.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The replay-delete test only changes a mocked fixture to None; the new None guard in _make_recording_filenames is never executed, so the test passes whether or not the behaviour is broken.
suggestions.suggestionContent: This test is the only place updated for the new `max_segment_id: None` handling, but it patches `delete_matched_rows`, so `_make_recording_filenames` (src/sentry/replays/usecases/delete.py:86-106) — where the new `if row["max_segment_id"] is None: return []` guard lives — is never reached. The fixture change from `0` to `None` therefore proves nothing: the test passes with the guard present or removed. Add a test that calls `_make_recording_filenames` (or `delete_replay_recordings`) directly with a row whose `max_segment_id` is `None` and asserts `[]` is returned and no storage deletes occur, so the None branch is actually exercised.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The rewritten hook can return `attributes: undefined` during the initial fetch and on error, where the previous implementation always returned an initialized TagCollection, so consumers that index it can throw.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Before this change `attributes` was built into a fresh object (`const allAttributes: TagCollection = {}`) so the hook always returned an object. The new implementation returns `attributes: isFetching ? previous : data` sourced directly from `useQuery`. `usePrevious(data, isFetching)` has no prior value to fall back on for the first fetch, and on the error path `isFetching` is false while `data` is `undefined` (the hook even exposes `error` now), so callers receive `undefined` where they previously received `{}`. Any caller doing `Object.keys(attributes)`, `Object.entries(attributes)`, `attributes[key]`, or spreading it into another TagCollection will throw at render. Keep the object contract by defaulting, e.g. `attributes: (isFetching ? previous : data) ?? {}` (and consider returning `{}` on error as well).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: useTraceItemAttributeKeys can now return undefined attributes where it previously guaranteed a TagCollection, dropping the `?? []` fallback.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The reworked hook returns `attributes: isFetching ? previous : data`, where `data` comes straight from `useQuery` and is `undefined` whenever the query is disabled or has errored (isFetching === false). The previous implementation derived `attributes` from `result.data ?? []` inside a `useMemo`, so callers were guaranteed a `TagCollection` (at least `{}`) once loading finished. The `?? []` fallback that covered the empty/error case was dropped. Any consumer that reads the result as an object (e.g. spread/Object.keys/mergeTags) can now receive `undefined` and throw. Preserve the old guarantee, e.g. `attributes: isFetching ? previous : (data ?? {})`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The test patches `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at line 15, which replaces `sleep` on the global `time` module for the whole test, so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` at line 62 (comment: 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change') is a no-op. WHY: The intended synchronization between the drift update and `step.join()` never happens, so the test still races the background flusher thread and can intermittently fail on `(msg,) = messages` when no segment has been produced yet. HOW: Use a synchronization primitive that is not patched (e.g. wait on an event/condition, or call the unpatched sleep via `import time; time.sleep.__wrapped__`/a separate alias captured before patching) instead of `time.sleep`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: wait_produce timer uses tag key "shards" while the sibling produce/segment_size metrics use "shard".
suggestions.suggestionContent: The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged with key `"shards"`, but every other metric added in this PR (`spans.buffer.flusher.produce` at line 185, `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` at line 195, and `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` at line 244) uses `"shard"`. Queries/dashboards that group or filter by `shard` will silently miss this timer, so its latency data will look absent for those panels. Use the same tag key (`"shard"`) for consistency.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: test_basic's added time.sleep is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched earlier in the same test.
suggestions.suggestionContent: This added `time.sleep(0.1)` is intended to "give flusher threads time to process after drift change", but line 15 of this same test does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which replaces the attribute on the shared `time` module. The call therefore returns immediately and never yields the wall-clock delay the comment relies on, so the statement is dead and the race it was meant to paper over is not actually addressed.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: _create_process_for_shard is dead code — only the plural _create_process_for_shards is ever called.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `_create_process_for_shard` (singular) is never referenced anywhere in the codebase; the live restart path calls `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) with a `process_index`. This singular method is dead code left over from the refactor and should be removed to avoid the false impression that per-shard restarts are supported.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: `max_processes or len(...)` treats an explicit 0 as absent, silently falling back to the full shard count.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` uses a truthiness test on an integer parameter. If anyone passes `flusher_processes=0` (e.g. via the new `--flusher-processes 0` option), 0 is falsy and is replaced by the total shard count instead of being honored. Use an explicit None check: `self.max_processes = len(buffer.assigned_shards) if max_processes is None else max_processes`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The added `time.sleep(0.1)` (line 62) is intended to "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change", but the test patched `time.sleep` to a no-op at line 15 (`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`). The same `time` module is used, so the call returns immediately and performs no waiting at all — the line is inert and the comment misdescribes what happens. If the intent is to gate on the background flusher having finished, synchronise on a condition (e.g. wait for `messages`/flusher state) rather than a `time.sleep` that this fixture neutralises.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The comment claims to "Verify shards are distributed across processes", but the assertion only checks `sum(len(shards) for shards in process_to_shards_map.values()) == 4`. That sum is `len(assigned_shards)` by construction (every shard is appended exactly once when the map is built), so it holds even if all 4 shards were assigned to a single process — a round-robin distribution bug would not be caught. Assert the per-process contents instead, e.g. `assert all(len(shards) > 0 for shards in flusher.process_to_shards_map.values())` and/or `assert sorted(len(shards) for shards in flusher.process_to_shards_map.values()) == [2, 2]`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The added sleep is neutralized by the earlier `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", ...)`, so the test still races the flusher thread.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The added `time.sleep(0.1)` is a no-op: `test_basic` sets `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at line 15, which replaces `time.sleep` module-wide for the entire test body, so the sleep intended to "give flusher threads time to process after drift change" never actually sleeps. The flusher runs in background threads (produce_to_pipe path uses `threading.Thread` in flusher.py:108), so without a real wait the flush triggered by mutating `current_drift` may not complete before `step.join()`, leaving the test racy/flaky. Use a synchronization primitive that is not patched (e.g. spin on the produced `messages`/a threading.Event, or use `time.sleep` from `time` obtained before patching) instead of relying on a monkeypatched sleep.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: join() no longer terminates the remaining flusher processes once the timeout is exceeded, whereas the old single-process join always terminated the process.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new join() loop breaks out of the per-process loop as soon as the deadline has elapsed (`if remaining_time <= 0: break`), which also skips the `process.terminate()` call for that process and every process after it. Previously termination was unconditional after the wait (the single process was always terminated even when the deadline had passed). A caller that calls join(timeout) during consumer shutdown now leaves flusher child processes alive (they only die with the parent), so the guarantee that join(timeout) stops the flusher processes on timeout is lost. Terminate the processes even when the deadline has passed, e.g. break/wait first but still run the terminate for every process (or terminate the current process before breaking).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Class docstring claims one process per shard, but the code caps processes and shares shards across them.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The docstring states "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the code this PR adds caps the process count at `max_processes` and round-robins shards onto the resulting processes (`num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))`, `process_index = i % self.num_processes` at lines 60-66). With `--flusher-processes=2` and 4 shards, only 2 processes are created and each handles 2 shards, as the new test asserts. The doc line is therefore false; a caller reading it would expect one process per shard. Update the docstring to describe the capped/shared-process behaviour.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The new isinstance guard checks multiprocessing.Process, which the declared spawn-process class does not subclass, so hung flusher processes are never killed.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new health-check guard tests `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`, but `process` is declared as `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess | threading.Thread` (flusher.py:68) and the processes built here come from `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process` (i.e. `SpawnProcess`). `SpawnProcess` and `multiprocessing.Process` are sibling subclasses of `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, so the check is always False for real flusher processes and `process.kill()` never runs. Before this PR `_ensure_process_alive` called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally, so a crashed/hung flusher process is now never reaped and a new one is spawned on every unhealthy pass (the identical guard also skips `process.terminate()` in join). Test for the concrete spawn class (or, when `produce_to_pipe is None`, for `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`) instead of `multiprocessing.Process`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: `queued` dataclass default is evaluated once at import, so all instances share the same timestamp.
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `queued` uses `timezone.now()` as a dataclass field default, which Python evaluates exactly once when the class body is defined (module import), so every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` gets the same timestamp instead of the moment the assignment was queued. WHY: the field is intended to record when the source was queued, but it actually records process start time — any analytics/debugging that reads `queued` (via `to_dict`) will report misleading values. HOW: use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so the timestamp is computed per instance: `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Abstract `sync_status_outbound` declares `assignment_source` that concrete overrides don't accept, so threading it would raise TypeError.
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: the abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature was changed to accept `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, but concrete overrides do not declare it (e.g. `ExampleIntegration.sync_status_outbound(self, external_issue, is_resolved, project_id)` at src/sentry/integrations/example/integration.py:161 has neither the param nor `**kwargs`). WHY: the parameter is added to signal that callers should thread the assignment source through (the PR's stated goal of blocking sync cycles), but any caller that passes `assignment_source=` per the new contract will raise `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument` on those installations. HOW: either thread the parameter through every concrete override (adding `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None, **kwargs`) or drop it from the abstract signature until implementations support it.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: `queued` default `timezone.now()` is frozen at import time, so all sources report the same timestamp instead of when they were queued.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a default argument evaluated once at class-definition (import) time, not per-instance. Every AssignmentSource created via `from_integration()` — which never supplies `queued` — therefore reports the same import-time timestamp instead of the moment the assignment was queued, making the field a meaningless measurement. Use a per-instance default, e.g. `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)` (importing `field` from `dataclasses`), so each source records its own creation time.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: A datetime field is placed into a Celery JSON payload via asdict(), which can raise at encode time on the queue boundary.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `AssignmentSource` carries a `datetime` field (`queued: datetime = timezone.now()`) and `to_dict()` returns `asdict(self)`, which preserves `queued` as a raw `datetime` object (asdict does not stringify datetimes). That dict is placed directly into a Celery payload in `sync_group_assignee_outbound` (`sync.py:141-143`, `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...)`), and the inbound path always builds a source via `AssignmentSource.from_integration(...)` (`sync.py:98,115`), so this payload is now routinely enqueued. If the task serializer's JSON encoder has no rule for `datetime`, the encode fails at `apply_async` (not at `to_dict()`), breaking inbound-assignee sync. Serialize `queued` as an ISO string in `to_dict()` (or make it a `str` field), e.g. `return {**asdict(self), 'queued': self.queued.isoformat()}`, and parse it back in `from_dict` so the round-trip type matches. Note also that `queued = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class definition, so all default instances share one timestamp — use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` if per-instance enqueue time is intended.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Test named for an empty array passes an empty dict, so the name disagrees with the body.
suggestions.suggestionContent: test_from_dict_empty_array is named for an empty *array*, but its body passes an empty *dict* ({}). If the intent was to verify from_dict on a list/array input, this never exercises that path — from_dict is annotated `input_dict: dict` and `cls(**{})` fails with TypeError for a different reason (missing required fields) than an array would. Either rename the test to test_from_dict_empty_dict or actually pass an array (e.g. from_dict([]), if supported) so the name matches the behaviour under test. The neighboring test_from_dict_inalid_data also has a typo in its name.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: `to_dict()` emits a datetime that the Celery serialization of `apply_async` kwargs cannot encode.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `to_dict()` returns `asdict(self)`, so `queued` is a raw `datetime`. That dict is handed to `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs={..., "assignment_source_dict": assignment_source.to_dict()})` in src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py:136-145, which serializes kwargs with the Celery task serializer; a `datetime` is not JSON-serializable, so the enqueue raises and the outbound assignee sync silently never runs. The consumer task then reconstructs via `AssignmentSource.from_dict`, which performs no datetime coercion. Make the value serializable, e.g. store `queued` as an ISO-8601 string (or exclude it from `to_dict`), so producer and serializer agree.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: `should_sync` gained a positional parameter that is now passed positionally, so subclass overrides using the old signature break.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The widened `should_sync` signature is consumed positionally at sync_assignee_outbound.py:56 (`installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)`). Reconstructed before the change, `should_sync` took a single `attribute`; subclasses that override it with that old signature will now raise TypeError when the updated task passes the second positional argument, silently breaking outbound assignee sync for those integrations. Make the added parameter keyword-only in the base definitions and pass it by keyword at the call site so existing one-parameter overrides remain compatible.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` is indexed unconditionally, but `"sender"` is optional in integration metadata — `build_integration` only sets it when `state.get("sender")` (line 376) and `installation.py:44` explicitly guards `if "sender" not in integration.metadata`. WHY: when an ACTIVE Integration with the matching external_id exists without an OrganizationIntegration but lacks `sender` metadata (e.g. a legacy integration created before the webhook wrote sender, or one whose org integration was removed), this line raises KeyError and returns a 500 instead of the intended `error()` page. HOW: use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` (or explicitly `return error(...)` when sender is absent) before comparing against `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Direct nested access to the conditionally-populated `metadata["sender"]["login"]` can raise KeyError/TypeError instead of returning the error dialog.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `metadata` is a JSON field and `sender` is written only conditionally (build_integration only sets metadata["sender"] when state.get("sender") is truthy), so `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` can raise an unhandled KeyError (or TypeError when sender is null) on an Integration that has no sender payload. That turns a case the surrounding code intends to funnel into the graceful `error(...)` dialog into a 500. Use a `.get("sender", {}).get("login")` chain (or explicitly guard for a missing sender and return `error(...)`).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Validator reads metadata["sender"]["login"] unconditionally while the writer sets "sender" only conditionally, so a missing sender raises KeyError instead of the intended error page.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The validity check indexes `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` unconditionally, but the site that writes this metadata (`build_integration`, lines 376-377) only sets `metadata["sender"]` when `state.get("sender")` is truthy. When an ACTIVE GitHub Integration was created without a sender in metadata (Integration exists, OrganizationIntegration does not), this branch executes and the key access raises KeyError, returning a 500 instead of the graceful `error(...)` page the check is meant to produce. Read the value defensively, e.g. `sender = integration.metadata.get("sender") or {}` and compare against `sender.get("login")`, so a missing sender yields the same "Invalid installation request." error rather than an unhandled exception.

If the existing Integration was created by a path that did not carry a sender, this subscript raises KeyError and returns a 500 instead of the graceful `error(...)` failure page the surrounding code uses. Read the value defensively, e.g. `sender = integration.metadata.get("sender") or {}` and compare against `sender.get("login")`, returning `error(request, self.active_organization)` when it is missing or does not match.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The new sender-verification reads integration.metadata["sender"]["login"], but build_integration only sets metadata["sender"] conditionally, so a missing key raises KeyError (500) instead of the intended failure page.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new check compares the OAuth-authenticated GitHub login against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. However `build_integration` (same file, ~line 376) only writes `metadata["sender"]` when `state.get("sender")` is truthy (the webhook-install path). For an Integration created through the normal pipeline (or any Integration whose metadata has no `sender`), this subscript raises KeyError and the request 500s instead of rendering the github-integration-failed page. Guard the lookup, e.g. `sender_login = integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing/empty value as a failed verification (or skip the check). Note also that the comparison is case-sensitive although GitHub logins are case-insensitive, which could falsely reject a legitimate installer whose login differs only in case — consider comparing lowercased values.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The OAuth state / pipeline signature token is compared with `!=`, a non-constant-time string comparison that can leak the token via timing.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The `state` value echoed back by GitHub is the `pipeline.signature` token generated at line 402 and sent in the authorize URL at line 408. Validating it with Python's `!=` short-circuits on the first differing byte, giving a timing side channel on a secret/CSRF token. Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. `from django.utils.crypto import constant_time_compare` and `constant_time_compare(request.GET.get("state"), pipeline.signature)`, or `hmac.compare_digest` with both operands as `str`/bytes of equal shape). This matches the requirement that comparisons of tokens/credentials use constant-time primitives.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: test_installation_not_found asserts a generic error string that OAuthLoginView emits before the 404-stubbed installation lookup is ever reached, so the test passes even if installation-not-found handling is broken.
suggestions.suggestionContent: test_installation_not_found is named after (and stubs) the missing-installation API 404, but it never reaches that code. It omits `_stub_github()`, so the OAuth token-exchange request to https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token is unmocked; safe_urlopen/read raises and integration.py:428-429 sets payload={}, causing line 431-432 to return the generic `error()` whose default text is "Invalid installation request." The final assertion at line 396 is therefore satisfied by the OAuthLoginView error path, and the same string is also produced by the state-mismatch (line 413) and user-mismatch (line 505) branches, so the assertion cannot tell which branch fired. The 404 stub on /app/installations/{id} is a no-op and the test would pass with installation-not-found handling removed entirely. Drive the flow far enough to actually call get_installation_info with the 404 in place (e.g. stub the OAuth token and /user responses via _stub_github so OAuthLoginView succeeds and the pipeline reaches the installation fetch), and assert a message unique to the missing-installation branch rather than the shared "Invalid installation request." default.

suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: get_failure_reason's docstring promises output the implementation does not produce.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The docstring's second example ("2 missed check-ins, 1 timeout check-in and 1 error check-in were detected") does not match what the function returns. With two missed, one timeout and one error, `status_counts` yields "2 missed", "1 timeout", "1 error"; `get_text_list(..., last_word=_("and"))` joins them into "2 missed, 1 timeout and 1 error"; and the suffix at line 156 is `_("%(problem_checkins)s check-ins detected")`, so the actual result is "2 missed, 1 timeout and 1 error check-ins detected" (no "were", and "check-ins" counted once over the whole list). The first example ("3 missed check-ins detected") matches only because the count happens to be one value. Since callers/readers treat this docstring as the contract for the evidence-display value, either fix the examples to the real output (e.g. "2 missed, 1 timeout and 1 error check-ins detected", "A missed check-in was detected") or adjust the formatting to match the documented phrasing.
